summary: Revises how BGP handles malformed attributes in UPDATE messages. Instead of resetting the whole session, as the base specification demanded, speakers can treat routes as withdrawn or ignore attributes, so other routes are not disrupted.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7606 changes how a BGP router reacts to a malformed route update. It can remove the routes in that update while keeping the session and other routes when it can safely identify them.

questions: how does bgp handle malformed update messages
subtitle: BGP can contain a malformed route update without dropping every route on the session.

tldr.problem: The original BGP rules closed a whole session when an UPDATE contained a malformed attribute. That also removed valid routes and could spread the effect of one bad attribute.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7606 ranks four responses and assigns a milder response to many errors: withdraw the routes in the affected UPDATE or discard an attribute that cannot change route selection.
tldr.outcome: The revised rules reduce disruption while retaining a session when the NLRI can be parsed safely. RFC 7606 is a Proposed Standard that updates eight BGP-related RFCs.

today: RFC 7606 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Bad Attribute Should Not Drop a Session
sections.content:
The base BGP specification, RFC 4271, requires a router to reset a session when an UPDATE contains a malformed attribute. A reset also removes valid routes exchanged on that session. Optional transitive attributes can travel through routers that do not recognize or check them, so the eventual reset may affect a router far from the source.

RFC 7606 aims to preserve the session and valid routes, while removing routes carried in the malformed UPDATE when possible. It updates error handling specified in several BGP attribute documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A malformed attribute can affect many routes if the router closes the whole BGP session. RFC 7606 limits the response to the affected update when the router can still identify its routes.

sections.title: Four Responses to an UPDATE Error
sections.content:
The RFC defines four responses, from strongest to weakest. A session reset sends a NOTIFICATION and ends the session. AFI/SAFI disable ignores later routes for one address-family and sub-address-family combination on that session. Treat-as-withdraw handles all routes in the UPDATE as withdrawn. Attribute discard removes the malformed attribute and continues processing.

A router may use attribute discard only when that attribute does not affect route selection or installation. If errors in one UPDATE require different responses, the router uses the strongest required response.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can close the session, stop accepting one address family, withdraw routes from one update, or discard one attribute. It chooses the strongest response required by the errors it found.

sections.title: How Error Handling Changes
sections.content:
A NOTIFICATION with the UPDATE Message Error code is required when the specified response is a session reset. A conflict in the Optional or Transitive attribute flag bits normally calls for treat-as-withdraw. Missing well-known mandatory attributes also call for treat-as-withdraw. For ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, MULTI_EXIT_DISC, and LOCAL_PREF, treat-as-withdraw replaces a reset in the specified cases; malformed ATOMIC_AGGREGATE and AGGREGATOR use attribute discard.

A repeated MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI still requires a NOTIFICATION. Later copies of other repeated attributes are discarded. Some excessive length errors retain their earlier handling. Treat-as-withdraw requires successful parsing of the route information; if the router cannot parse it, it must reset the session or disable the address family as applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: Most listed attribute errors no longer require ending the session. The router withdraws affected routes or discards a safe-to-ignore attribute, but it still resets the session when it cannot locate routes reliably.

sections.title: Locating Routes in an UPDATE
sections.content:
The Total Attribute Length can disagree with lengths inside the attributes. In specified conflicts, the router uses treat-as-withdraw and relies on the Total Attribute Length to locate the start of NLRI. A zero-length attribute is invalid unless its definition permits it; this RFC names AS_PATH and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE as valid zero-length cases.

For new messages, MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI, when present, is placed first among path attributes. An UPDATE must not carry more than one of the listed non-empty route fields. Receivers must still accept older message arrangements. The RFC also defines invalid NLRI lengths and requires unrecognized typed NLRI to be discarded unless another specification says otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The router must know where route information begins before it can withdraw the right routes. RFC 7606 sets length and placement rules to make that boundary easier to find, while keeping receivers compatible with older layouts.

sections.title: Operational Effects and New Attribute Rules
sections.content:
Treat-as-withdraw on an internal BGP session can make routing inconsistent within an autonomous system. Possible effects include forwarding loops, unreachable destinations, or less direct routes. The RFC considers this less harmful than resetting the session, and recommends tracing affected routes to their ingress router and filtering the source there. A speaker must log the involved NLRI and the complete malformed UPDATE for debugging.

Authors defining a new BGP attribute must specify what makes it malformed and how to handle that error. Treat-as-withdraw is generally preferred; session reset is discouraged. Attribute discard needs careful analysis if the attribute could affect route selection or installation.
sections.plainLanguage: Withdrawing routes can still cause temporary routing problems inside a network. Operators need logs that identify the affected routes, and authors of new attributes must define clear error handling.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The revised handling addresses a case where an attacker sends a malformed optional transitive attribute. Routers that do not recognize it may pass it along, and later routers that do recognize it may reset sessions. Propagation can multiply the damage.

The RFC also warns that error responses could expose reactions if BGP were protected by a confidentiality-only mechanism without data integrity. It recommends authenticated encryption and discarding messages that fail verification. In other respects, it says BGP's security characteristics do not change.
sections.plainLanguage: A malformed attribute can travel through routers before one detects it. RFC 7606 reduces the resulting disruption and says messages that fail security checks should be discarded.

viz.caption: The four responses, from strongest to weakest

items.title: Session reset
items.text: Send a NOTIFICATION and end the BGP session.

items.title: AFI/SAFI disable
items.text: Ignore later routes for one address family on the session.

items.title: Treat-as-withdraw
items.text: Remove routes in the malformed UPDATE as withdrawn.

items.title: Attribute discard
items.text: Discard the attribute and keep processing the UPDATE.
